claims.text: Thermal exposure causes Mg to diffuse from the metastable matrix to grain boundaries and intermetallic interfaces.
Interfacial Mg enrichment triggers the transformation of unstable intermetallic phases into thermodynamically more stable Mg-containing compounds.
Thermal treatment produces a more uniform microstructure with refined, stable intermetallic phases.
Mg-enriched regions oxidize to form a coherent, adherent, Mg-rich oxide or passivation film.
The Mg-rich oxide film reduces the number of active corrosion sites.
Mg-mediated segregation and oxide formation improve corrosion resistance.
Mg-mediated segregation and oxide formation improve high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial alloy is a rapidly solidified, induction-melted Mg-containing lightweight HEA.
The initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
The initial alloy contains a metastable primary solid solution and dispersed intermetallic compounds.
The as-cast baseline has a heterogeneous distribution of metastable phases.
The as-cast baseline lacks significant Mg segregation and a well-developed protective oxide film.
Temperatures above approximately 300 degrees C are sufficient to activate the diffusion needed for the proposed evolution.
The proposed mechanism applies only when treatment does not cause complete homogenization or uncontrolled phase separation.
Extreme thermal exposure or composition changes may produce behavior different from the proposed mechanism.
Annealing will shift the corrosion potential to less negative values relative to the as-cast baseline.
Annealing will lower corrosion current density relative to the as-cast baseline.
Annealing will reduce the high-temperature oxidation rate relative to the as-cast baseline.
Processing and composition can synergistically affect corrosion resistance in Mg-rich compositionally complex alloys.
The kinetics of Mg diffusion and quantitative phase-stability evolution in the proposed alloy are unresolved.
